extracted.intended_audience: short-story writers, magazine editors, and literary critics (authors, editors, and publishers of short fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial selection criteria and principles for choosing the year's best American short stories and for curating an anthology; includes standards for judging quality and guidance to magazine editors and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of Substance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first test of a short story, therefore, in any qualitative analysis is to report upon how vitally compelling the writer makes his selected facts or incidents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance is 'something achieved by the artist in every act of creation' and not merely facts; it obtains substantial embodiment when 'the artist's power of compelling imaginative persuasion transforms them into a living truth.' The editor values 'essential human qualities' and 'psychological and imaginative reality' in substance. Anti-pattern: 'inorganic fiction' (fiction lacking an organic pulse of life) is a curse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of Form
rubrics_metrics.description: "The true artist will seek to shape this living substance into the most beautiful and satisfying form, by skilful selection and arrangement of his material, and by the most direct and appealing presentation of it in portrayal and characterization."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form is judged by selection, arrangement, portrayal, and characterization; shaping substance into an appealing, coherent artistic whole elevates a story above others and contributes to its lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double standard: substance and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Each story is tested by the 'double standard of substance and form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor examines each story impartially and grants the writer's chosen point of view, then evaluates whether the story succeeds on substance (imaginative, organic life) and on form (artistic shaping, presentation). Surviving both tests is necessary for higher rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-group classification / asterisk ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are classified into four groups indicated in the yearbook index by asterisks: no asterisk, one (*), two (**), or three (***).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group definitions: (1) fail to survive either the test of substance or form — listed without comment or asterisk; (2) survive either substance or form — indicated by a single asterisk; (3) survive both tests and may 'lay convincing claim to a second reading' — indicated by two asterisks; (4) unite genuine substance and artistic form in a closely woven pattern and 'may fairly claim a position in our literature' — indicated by three asterisks and listed in the Rolls of Honor. The stories reprinted in the anthology are selected from the final list (***).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic-substance requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: "No substance is of importance in fiction, unless it is organic substance, that is to say, substance in which the pulse of life is beating."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substance must feel alive and organic; mere factual or inorganic material without imaginative transformation is insufficient. 'Inorganic fiction' is explicitly criticized as harmful to literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological and imaginative reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should confer 'psychological and imaginative reality' upon their material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor prizes work that renders life imaginatively and convincingly so that readers respond with part of their own experience; this quality is central to the test of substance and to chronicling 'the fresh living current' in contemporary fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial examination and methodological approach
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have taken each short story by itself, and examined it impartially. I have done my best to surrender myself to the writer's point of view..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluator should grant the writer's choice of material and personal interpretation, then apply the double standard. The editor asserts he permitted 'no personal preference or prejudice to influence my judgment consciously,' though he admits some personal preferences occasionally appear in the asterisking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns: wordiness and commercial standardization
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazine practices that encourage 'wordiness' and 'commercial standardization' are identified as causes of poor short-story quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary M. Colum's remedy (quoted) is for editors to decline stories over 3,000 words and refuse to pay more than $100; O'Brien modifies this recommendation to: except in unusual instances limit stories to 5,000 words and compensation should not exceed $300. Rationale: shorter/pay-limited policy would raise literary standards and attract imaginative writers rather than commercial exploiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial anthology rules (originality & author-coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor's stated rules for the anthology: he will not republish an English story or a translation from a foreign author and 'has also made it a rule not to include more than one story by an individual author in the volume.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are firm inclusion policies intended to emphasize American work and broaden representation among authors. Also, stories in the volume are arranged alphabetically and that order does not indicate comparative merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection does not equal greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: "My selection of them does not imply the critical belief that they are great stories."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion (even in the top group) is characterized as finding the equivalent of six volumes 'worthy of republication' among the year's stories, not a definitive pronouncement of greatness; this tempers claim of judgement and frames selection as a conservative, documentary act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial mission: chronicle first signs of grace / focus on emerging work
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor's stated function is 'to begin at the bottom and record the first signs of grace, rather than to limit myself to the top and write critically about work which will endure with or without criticism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluator/anthologist should value discovery and documentation of promising work across the field, not only already-established masterpieces; this supports including lesser-known but distinctive pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended critical practice for literary critics
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor urges critics to 'devote their attention for ten years to this spade work' of chronicling and evaluating a wide range of short fiction rather than only high-profile works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term, ground-level critical labor is recommended to 'clear the atmosphere' and enable permanent literary criticism; this is guidance for critical methodology rather than a story-by-story metric.
